 Our tax system should be as fair as it can possibly be
 Tom Maguire 
 21:00 
 This year’s budget was all about making your money work harder for you. We saw good moves with the new investment account and other provisions.
 We also saw some changes in relation to making certain tax deductions for the cost of borrowing more straightforward. For example, when it comes to interest deductions, just say “section 247” to any tax adviser and watch their reaction; so the process of simplification has started.
 Making your (or borrowed) money work harder for you in tax terms of this is fair. But what about when tax isn’t fair? I’ve written about that previously. I’ve lost count of the many cases that have come before the Tax Appeal Commission (a form of tax court) where “out of time” tax refund claims have been denied.
 There is a period of four years for which a refund must be claimed; outside that period then the taxpayer gets zip. When a taxpayer overpays tax then it is their money owed back but that doesn’t matter at the Cinderella-hour at the end of the fourth year.
 There are many reasons why a taxpayer might not get to make a refund claim within that period. Life might just have gotten in the way such that a tax refund was the last thing on the taxpayer’s mind.
 Consider one case from earlier this year. The taxpayer filed a tax return for 2020 on November 18 2025 with Revenue. The return indicated that the taxpayer had overpaid income tax for 2020 in the amount of €9,500.
 The claim for repayment of income tax had not been made within four years of the end of the relevant tax year to which the claim related pursuant to the provisions of the relevant tax law. Revenue disallowed repayment of the overpaid tax for 2020 on that basis.
 The taxpayer explained that he was not aware of the four year rule which was referred to in Revenue’s letter. I wonder what percentage of the population (excluding tax nerds) would be so aware?
 Further he also had difficult personal circumstances as his wife had undergone surgery, he had a son who was very ill and the taxpayer was going through lots of medical tests which required him to travel on numerous occasions.
 The relevant tax period occurred during the pandemic and he did not apply to receive the government payments which were available during this time.
 So you can understand why the claim was late: life mattered, tax did not.
 The Tax Appeals Commissioner explained: “This is an unfortunate situation, and the Commissioner has every sympathy with the Appellant's position and the reasons why the claim for repayment was not made within the relevant time period. However, the Commissioner has no discretion in these cases due to the application of the four year rule.”
 A similar four-year time limit presents itself where the taxpayer has not paid enough tax but there are exceptions from Revenue’s perspective. If the taxpayer had been fraudulent or negligent in completing their tax return then that time limit is disapplied.
 If that taxpayer did not make a full and true disclosure on a tax return then that time limit is also disapplied. Recent court cases in connection with the meaning of true and full disclosure have arguably elevated the importance of that test.
 My point here is that there are exceptions to the four-year limit where the taxpayer owes money but not the other way around. Therefore the solution would be to bring in a reasonableness test such that the “access denied” response to refunds will be put aside where there are reasonable grounds for the claim being late.
 Another example on fairness is one which I wrote about in these pages previously was one where the Commissioner noted the “unfortunate situation where the appellant did not appreciate the impact which his decision to reduce the amount of the mortgage draw down from €220,000 to €200,000 would have on his eligibility for the Help to Buy scheme”.
 It went on: “Had the Appellant drawn down €203,000 of a mortgage he would have fallen within the terms of the Help to Buy scheme”.
 Here the taxpayer made a decision to reduce his financial risk in buying a house but increased the tax risk as a result. This is one instance where the tax tail could have wagged the commercial dog, which goes against the purpose of tax law in the first instance.
 The reasonableness suggestion would also hold in this instance. Don’t get me wrong, the exchequer has both the right and responsibility to protect its resources and therefore cannot be allowed to entertain refund claims going back to the dawn of time.
 Flexibility in the case of financial hardship is not new to our tax law; certain taxes are allowed by instalments or certain interim refunds of withholding tax can be claimed where the taxpayer can demonstrate hardship.
 It is unlikely that we will see such changes in this year’s Finance Bill process, although never say never. Therefore it’s so important that you make all claims on time, and that all of your tax returns meet the full and true disclosure test and that you tick all boxes appropriately.
 Tom Maguire is a tax partner in Deloitte and adjunct full professor at UCD Smurfit School
